items.title: Chief Technology Officer (Machine Learning & Computer Vision)
bullets: By September 2025 the one-shot detection prototypes worked well enough that the open question stopped being "can this detect defects" and became "can a customer run this unattended on their line" — I took the CTO title because that shift needed one person accountable for the whole path from model to deployed system, not a hand-off after the model was done.

Getting there meant re-deriving the ONNX export and quantization path for five PyTorch models myself and wiring the output into a Django/WebSocket service; the number that mattered to the customer was inspection setup time falling from 33 minutes to under 53 seconds, not model accuracy in isolation.

In production the models ran at the camera's full 25 FPS. Benchmarked on their own they reached 94 FPS, so once inference was optimized the bottleneck was camera capture and stream handling, not the model — more model tuning would not have moved the line rate.

For the QMS, I chose Ollama and a local RAG pipeline on PostgreSQL/pgvector over a cloud LLM on purpose — it's slower and less sharp than a hosted frontier model, but it meant SOP documents never left the customer's network, which mattered more than raw answer quality on an ISO 9001 shop floor. Every answer had to cite the SOP passage it came from, and when retrieval found nothing relevant the system said so instead of guessing.

Leading six engineers changed what I spent my own time on: less hands-on code, more review and architecture calls. The CAPA/SPC/PPAP automation and the semantic PDF comparison tool were mostly built by the team under direction I set, not code I wrote end to end.

items.title: R&D Scientist — Computer Vision & Deep Learning
bullets: At Therness R&D, data scarcity was the core challenge: standard CV models failed on thermal datasets. I focused on one-shot and low-data learning.
I built foundational algorithms that could detect defects with minimal examples and established a rigorous error-analysis workflow to harden models for field use.
This phase was about deep problem-solving and validating that the technology was viable before scaling to production.

items.title: Algorithm Development for Weld Path Optimization | Data Scientist Intern
bullets: At Ades Consulting, I tackled the geometric challenge of automating weld paths by processing raw STL meshes to generate optimal robotic trajectories.
I developed a custom pipeline that analyzed mesh topology to predict the most efficient weld path, achieving a ~87% match rate with expert human trajectories.
The project sharpened my computational geometry and algorithm design skills, moving beyond pixel-based CV to vector-based spatial reasoning.

items.title: Statistical Analyst (Market Research)
bullets: At Shomal Market Insights, I learned the importance of data integrity while analyzing large survey datasets at scale.
Standard tools were too slow, so I optimized critical data-processing steps in C++ to improve runtime and reliability.
This experience marked my shift from a statistician analyzing the past to an engineer building tools for the future.

items.title: Data Analyst Intern
bullets: At the University of Hormozgan, I analyzed 10 years of data from 5,000+ students to uncover employment drivers.
Using statistical modeling, I proposed curriculum interventions; employment rates improved by 8.4% after implementation.
It cemented my belief that rigorous data analysis translates directly into real-world impact.

items.title: Edge Anomaly Inspection
items.status: Public — code, results and benchmark on GitHub
items.tagline: Visual defect detection that learns only from images of good parts, packaged as a single ONNX model and benchmarked on every backend I could run it on, with each latency number reported next to the accuracy it costs.
items.stack: Python · PyTorch · ONNX Runtime · CoreML · TensorRT · scikit-learn

narrative.heading: Why this project
body: In factory inspection the hard constraint is rarely the model. Defect examples barely exist when a line starts, and whatever runs has to fit the hardware already sitting next to the camera. I wanted a public project that takes both constraints seriously, on data anyone can check: the VisA PCB dataset (Amazon Science, CC BY 4.0).

narrative.heading: One graph: image in, anomaly map out
body: The method is PatchCore. Patch features from a frozen ImageNet backbone are stored as a memory bank of what normal looks like, thinned with greedy coreset selection, and every test patch is scored by its distance to the nearest normal one. No defect images are used for training.

The engineering decision was what to export. The official PatchCore code runs the nearest-neighbour search with FAISS, outside the network, which is one more dependency to install, version and get wrong on a production PC. I wrote the feature pooling as a fixed matrix and the search as a single matrix multiply, so the backbone, the projection and the scoring export together as one ONNX graph. The target machine needs an ONNX runtime and nothing else.

narrative.heading: What the measurements said
body: All numbers come from one run on an Apple M4, on the 200-image pcb1 test set (half of it defective), with every backend scored on the same images.

points.label: Accuracy.
points.text: Image-level AUROC 0.936, pixel-level AUROC 0.995. Building the memory bank from all 904 normal training images instead of a 200-image sample, at a similar bank size, moved image AUROC from 0.914 to 0.936.

points.label: GPU.
points.text: Fastest path: 23.8 ms per image in PyTorch on the M4 GPU (MPS), and 28.5 ms for the exported ONNX model on CoreML.

points.label: CPU, the result I didn't expect.
points.text: ONNX Runtime was slower than plain PyTorch on the M4's CPU (42.3 vs 34.5 ms), and INT8 quantization only brought it back to parity (35.2 ms). What INT8 did deliver was a model less than half the size, 135 MB down to 61 MB, for an image-AUROC cost of 0.007.

narrative.heading: What I took from it
body: "Quantize it and it gets faster" is a claim about a specific processor, not a property of the model. PyTorch on Apple Silicon already uses well-tuned CPU kernels, so there was little left for ONNX Runtime to win. That is why the repository ships the benchmark rather than a headline number: one command reruns the whole comparison on the hardware that will actually be on the line.

narrative.heading: What I'd do next
body: The defects the model is least sure about are the small ones, such as thin trace damage or a single bent pin, because a 224-pixel input throws away the detail they live in. Higher input resolution or tiling is the first experiment. The Jetson path, a TensorRT FP16 build script in the repo, has not been run on real hardware yet, so I don't quote numbers for it.

items.title: NeuroLingo
items.status: Core complete — 212 tests passing. Voice shadowing in progress.
items.tagline: An English-learning app for Farsi speakers, built around second-language acquisition research rather than flashcard convention: vocabulary is taught in whole sentences, never in isolation; reading is click-to-define; review scheduling is driven by spaced retrieval.
items.stack: Python · Flet/Flutter · SQLite · llama.cpp · NumPy · PyInstaller

narrative.heading: The constraint
body: The target user may have no reliable internet and no API budget. That single requirement invalidated the standard architecture. A cloud-only LLM was out. So was the conventional RAG stack — FAISS plus sentence-transformers pulls in PyTorch, which is hundreds of megabytes to gigabytes before a single line of application code. For something intended to ship as a mobile binary, that is disqualifying.
So the interesting work here was subtractive: what can be removed and still leave the system functional?

narrative.heading: LLM routing with graceful degradation
body: Rather than commit to a vendor, I defined an abstract LLMProvider contract and implemented it four times — Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, and a local GGUF model served through llama.cpp.

A router sits above them and walks the chain, catching authentication and availability failures specifically rather than swallowing every exception, and terminating at local inference. The app degrades in quality when offline; it does not stop working.
Providers are injected through the constructor, so the entire routing path — including every failure branch — is testable against fakes without touching a live API.

narrative.heading: Retrieval without the ML stack
body: I replaced the standard RAG components with two much smaller pieces:

points.label: Embeddings by hashing.
points.text: Text is tokenized into unigrams and bigrams, each token hashed into one of 4096 buckets, and the resulting vector L2-normalized. It is measurably less semantically sharp than a neural embedding — that is the honest tradeoff. In exchange it is deterministic, requires no training data, no model download, and no inference cost.

points.label: Vector store as a matrix.
points.text: Vectors live in a NumPy array; similarity search is one matrix multiply against the normalized query. No index structure, no FAISS. At the scale this app operates on — a personal sentence deck, well under ten thousand entries — an index would cost more in complexity than it returns in latency.

body: Net dependency footprint for the entire retrieval path: NumPy.

narrative.heading: Learning engine
body: SM-2 in pure Python — the algorithm behind Anki — tracking per-card ease factors and intervals across four grading levels. Zero dependencies, 41 unit tests.

Persistence is hand-written SQL over sqlite3 behind a repository abstraction: one class owns every query in the codebase. Connections are wrapped in a context manager that commits, rolls back, and closes without exception. WAL journaling for concurrent reads, cascading foreign keys, and an append-only review log so learning history can be reconstructed rather than inferred.
No ORM — for the same reason as no PyTorch. SQLite ships with Python.

narrative.heading: What I'd do differently
body: The hashing embeddings are the weakest link. They handle lexical overlap well and semantic paraphrase poorly, which limits how useful retrieval is for a learner asking a question in their own words. A small quantized embedding model would close most of that gap at an acceptable size cost, and is the next thing I want to measure rather than assume.

items.title: Master's Thesis — One-Shot Learning for Thermographic Weld Inspection
items.subtitle: In collaboration with Therness S.r.l.
items.status: Completed — contributed to March 2026 M.Sc. graduation
items.stack: PyTorch · OpenCV · Self-supervised learning · Edge inference (Jetson/TensorRT)
items.confidentialNote: Code and data are confidential — Therness production dataset.

narrative.heading: Why not just collect more labels
body: At Therness, every labeled thermal defect image starts as a confirmed physical failure — someone has to find and verify a bad weld before it becomes a training example. That doesn't scale with a production timeline, so the real research question wasn't "which classifier performs best" but whether a model could learn what a normal weld's thermal signature looks like from mostly unlabeled sequences, and flag deviations from that, instead of needing an example of every failure mode in advance.

narrative.heading: Self-supervised features over a supervised classifier
body: I pretrained on unlabeled thermal sequences with self-supervised learning to build the feature space, then layered one-shot / low-data detection on top using only a handful of labeled reference examples. The tradeoff is explicit: this setup can flag defect types the labeled set never saw, which a supervised classifier structurally cannot do, but its decision boundary is noisier than a model trained directly on labeled failures. I chose to accept that noise in exchange for not being blind to novel defects.

narrative.heading: Edge deployment was a constraint from day one, not an afterthought
body: The inspection line couldn't depend on network connectivity or send thermal footage off-site, so the model had to run in real time on an on-prem edge device. That meant designing the CV preprocessing and inference pipeline around TensorRT-level optimization from the start — treating latency and memory as first-class requirements during model selection, not something to fix after the fact.

narrative.heading: What's still open
body: A weld's "normal" thermal signature drifts with material batch and ambient temperature, so there's still a manual QA checklist step before each production run to catch drift the model hasn't seen. If I extended this work, I'd turn that into a monitored drift metric instead of a pre-run checklist — the current version depends on someone remembering to look at it.

about.title: About
intro: I trained as a statistician before I trained as an engineer, so my default question about any model is what it gets wrong and how often — not just whether it works on the demo.
Most of the decisions in my work are about matching a system's complexity to its actual constraints, instead of defaulting to whatever tool is fashionable.

sections.heading: Why I moved from R&D into ownership
body: I spent a year at Therness proving that one-shot and low-data learning could work on thermal welding data — the research question was real, and it took real time to answer honestly.

Once the prototypes worked, the harder problem stopped being modeling and became everything downstream of it: getting a model onto an edge device with no network dependency, building the service layer around it, and being the person a customer could actually hold accountable for the system running unattended on their line. I took the CTO title because I wanted to own that whole path, not hand it off after the interesting part was done.

sections.heading: What "production-grade" actually means to me
body: It doesn't mean the highest-accuracy model. It means the model plus everything that has to be true around it: it degrades instead of failing when the network is down, it doesn't send a customer's documents to a cloud API when privacy matters more than raw answer quality, and someone other than me can debug it at 2am.

The two projects on this page are both examples of that same question — what does this system actually need, and what can I honestly leave out — applied to very different constraints: an industrial edge device with a hard network requirement, and a phone with no internet at all.

sections.heading: What I'm looking for
body: An AI/ML engineering role in Italy or the Netherlands where the model has to work under real constraints: edge hardware, private data, unreliable networks, or a customer who needs it to run without someone watching.
I have about two years of hands-on work behind me, so I'm early in my career. I'd rather join a team where I can learn from people who have shipped more than I have, and take on more as I earn it.
